opening_message:
Ticket 1: Casey Wu (employee ID E005) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E005.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Casey Wu (E005) is a full-time Payroll Specialist requesting write access to Source Code. As a full-time employee, write is permitted (admin would require owning the system, which is not the case here). Recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E005 (Casey Wu) is a contractor with basic security training (note: this conflicts with the HR note saying full-time). Contractors max at read without advanced training. Requested write exceeds the maximum, so recommend granting read.
reason: Casey Wu (E005) requests write access to Source Code. HR note claims full-time (max write), but Security DB note independently lists E005 as a contractor with basic security training, explicitly flagging the conflict. Under policy, contractors without advanced training max at read, and the requested write exceeds that maximum. Given the conflicting employment records, I grant the more restrictive, safe level: read.

- full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system.
- contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.
